content: The health benefits of physical activity in preventing and managing a wide range of diseases are well-documented. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that adults engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity per week, performed in bouts of at least 10 minutes. The Exercise is Medicine initiative, which began in the United States and has since gained global traction, advocates for primary care providers to incorporate physical activity into patient care plans and offers resources to facilitate this. Similar approaches have been proposed in Europe. Various interventions have been studied in primary care settings to promote physical activity. Both counseling and prescribing physical activity have been shown to effectively increase patients' activity levels. A Cochrane systematic review evaluated interventions such as group exercise sessions, workshops, face-to-face counseling, phone calls, and written materials, finding a generally positive and moderate effect. Increasingly, studies are focusing on the role of interdisciplinary teams in delivering physical activity interventions. The costs of these interventions in primary care are comparable to those of pharmaceutical treatments, and in many cases, exercise may serve as a viable alternative to drug therapy. For example, the number needed to treat (NNT) to achieve physical activity recommendations through a combination of advice, written materials, and referrals is estimated at 12 sedentary adults. This is significantly lower than the NNT for smoking cessation advice, which ranges from 50 to 120. Many common medical and surgical interventions have NNTs higher than 12. Despite these findings, healthcare professionals (HCPs) do not consistently address physical activity in routine practice. In 2010, only 32.4% of adults in the United States reported being advised by an HCP to begin or continue exercising within the past year. Globally, similar trends are observed. For instance, only 37% of Korean primary care providers reported consistently collecting physical activity data from patients, and Australian general practitioners counseled only about 30% of their patients on physical activity weekly. Even when physical activity is discussed, the advice is often not actionable. In the United States, only 38% of patients who received physical activity advice were supported in developing a specific plan, and only 42% received follow-up support. Observational studies in Ohio family practices found that physical activity counseling lasted an average of just 47 seconds. Barriers to providing physical activity advice include lack of time, insufficient knowledge or training in physical activity counseling, and low confidence in influencing patient behavior. For example, a survey of Canadian family physicians revealed that 17% did not feel qualified to offer exercise advice, and only 4.9% had specialized knowledge in exercise science or counseling. Additional barriers include the absence of economic incentives, protocols for prescribing physical activity, and organizational support. A systematic review highlighted the importance of intervention materials, such as educational booklets and physical activity prescription aids, which are more likely to be used if they are adaptable to specific patients and perceived as evidence-based. Sedentary behavior and physical inactivity are significant public health concerns. In England, only 37% of men and 25% of women meet recommended physical activity levels. In Canada, these figures drop to 17% for men and 14% for women. In the United States, 23.1% of men and 15.8% of women meet physical activity guidelines. Globally, 31.1% of adults are estimated to be sedentary, with regional variations: 27.5% in Africa, 43.3% in the Americas, 43.2% in the Eastern Mediterranean, 34.8% in Europe, 17% in Southeast Asia, and 33.7% in the Western Pacific. Women are generally less active than men, with inactivity rates of 33.9% compared to 27.9%. Additionally, individuals in higher-income countries are more likely to be inactive than those in lower-income countries. To address these issues, studies have explored interventions aimed at encouraging HCPs to more consistently provide physical activity advice. These interventions include training, economic incentives, and audit and feedback mechanisms. Systemic approaches, such as creating resources for promoting physical activity and tools for screening and addressing sedentary behavior, have also been considered. Interventions targeting HCP behavior aim to equip them with the tools, resources, and strategies needed to effectively promote physical activity among patients. Systematic reviews have identified several barriers to changing HCP behavior regarding physical activity advice. These include attitudes, knowledge and skills, organizational and professional support, availability of community resources, and competing priorities. Successful interventions will likely need to address multiple barriers simultaneously. Although guidelines for physical activity promotion are well-established, evidence suggests that HCPs do not consistently implement these recommendations in practice. The effectiveness of interventions designed to encourage HCPs to adopt these strategies remains unclear. Numerous barriers hinder HCPs' ability to provide physical activity advice, and it is uncertain whether addressing some or all of these barriers is necessary to achieve meaningful behavior change. The goal of this research is to quantify the effects of specific interventions aimed at changing HCP behavior in delivering physical activity recommendations. By identifying and building upon best practices, future research can develop more effective interventions to increase physical activity levels among patients.
